content: Mitochondrial Eve, also known as mt-MRCA (mitochondrial most recent common ancestor), is the term used by researchers to describe the woman who is the matrilineal most recent common ancestor of all living humans. Her mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is passed exclusively from mothers to their offspring, has been inherited by all living humans today. This means that every mtDNA sequence in every living person can be traced back to her. Mitochondrial Eve is the matrilineal counterpart to Y-chromosomal Adam, the patrilineal most recent common ancestor of all living humans. However, they did not live at the same time. Mitochondrial Eve is estimated to have lived approximately 140,000 years ago in what is now Ethiopia, Kenya, or Tanzania. This estimation is based on the molecular clock technique, which correlates genetic drift with elapsed time. It is important to note that Mitochondrial Eve is not the unqualified most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of all humanity. While all living humans can trace their ancestry to the MRCA through at least one parent, Mitochondrial Eve can only be reached through the maternal lineage. Consequently, she lived much earlier than the MRCA of all humanity. The existence of Mitochondrial Eve and Y-chromosomal Adam does not imply that there were population bottlenecks or a first couple. Both lived within large human populations at different times. Some of their contemporaries left no living descendants, while others are ancestors of all people alive today. None of their contemporaries are ancestors of only a subset of living humans, as both Mitochondrial Eve and Y-chromosomal Adam lived long before the identical ancestors point, a time when all humans can be divided into those who left no descendants and those who are common ancestors of everyone alive today. Mitochondrial Eve is identified through matrilineal descent, which follows the inheritance of mtDNA exclusively from mothers. To trace back to Mitochondrial Eve, one would start with all living individuals and trace their maternal lineage backward in time. As one goes further back, the number of mitochondrial ancestors decreases until only one remains—Mitochondrial Eve. Similarly, tracing forward in time from Mitochondrial Eve, some of her contemporaries left no descendants, while others left only male descendants. Over time, most maternal lineages became extinct, leaving only one lineage that connects all living humans to Mitochondrial Eve. A common misconception is that Mitochondrial Eve was the only living human female of her time. This is incorrect. She lived among many other women, some of whom also have living descendants today. However, what distinguishes Mitochondrial Eve is that she has a purely matrilineal line of descent to all living humans, whereas her contemporaries have at least one male in every line of descent. Because mtDNA is passed exclusively through maternal descent, all humans alive today have mtDNA that can be traced back to Mitochondrial Eve. Mitochondrial Eve is estimated to have lived over 100,000 years before the identical ancestors point, which is thought to have occurred between 5,000 and 15,000 years ago. At this point in time, all humans can be divided into those who left no descendants and those who are common ancestors of everyone alive today. The study of Mitochondrial Eve is made possible by the unique inheritance of mitochondria, which are passed only from mothers to offspring. Each mitochondrion contains mtDNA, which mutates at a higher rate than nuclear DNA. This higher mutation rate provides researchers with a magnified view of genetic diversity within populations. Unlike nuclear DNA, which undergoes recombination from both parents, mtDNA is inherited solely from the mother, making it easier to trace maternal lineages. The concept of Mitochondrial Eve is often linked to the Out-of-Africa theory, which posits that all modern humans originated in Africa. Fossil and genetic evidence support this hypothesis. Phylogenetic trees constructed from mtDNA comparisons show that the earliest branching lineages belong to indigenous Africans, while lineages from other continents branch off from African lines. This suggests that all living humans descend from African populations, some of whom migrated out of Africa to populate the rest of the world. While mtDNA evidence supports the Out-of-Africa model, it does not indicate a population bottleneck. Different genetic trees, including those based on nuclear DNA, show varying coalescent points, suggesting extensive gene flow between populations even after the initial migration out of Africa. This idea is central to Alan Templeton's Out of Africa Again and Again theory. Criticisms of the original study on Mitochondrial Eve by Cann, Stoneking, and Wilson include limited sampling of sub-Saharan Africans, reliance on midpoint rooting for the phylogenetic tree, and the use of restriction-fragment length polymorphism, which is not ideal for estimating mutation rates. Subsequent studies, such as that by Ingman et al. in 2000, addressed these issues by sampling a more diverse population, sequencing complete mtDNA, and using outgroup rooting with chimpanzee mtDNA. These studies confirmed the major conclusions of Cann et al., supporting an African origin of human mtDNA within the past 172,000 ± 50,000 years. In popular culture, Mitochondrial Eve has inspired books, documentaries, and fictional works. For example, Bryan Sykes' The Seven Daughters of Eve explores human ancestry, while Richard Dawkins' River Out of Eden discusses Mitochondrial Eve in the context of genetic inheritance. The Discovery Channel's documentary The Real Eve and the Japanese novel and film series Parasite Eve also draw on the concept of Mitochondrial Eve.
